title: Locality and filter design for dissipative ground-state preparation
abstract: Ground-state preparation is a fundamental challenge in quantum many-body physics, chemistry and materials science. Dissipative state-preparation techniques engineer a Lindbladian coupling to a bath that drives the system to its ground state, needing no initial overlap. Their cost is dominated by the Hamiltonian simulations inside the filtered jump operators, since each jump is a weighted sum of Heisenberg-evolved copies, or branches, of a coupling operator. We reduce this cost by following three simple observations to their logical end. First, on a fixed time grid, linear programming optimises the branch weights, trading the heating response against the circuit cost. Second, Lieb--Robinson bounds let each branch evolve on a patch whose radius grows with its duration. Third, if the dynamics converges quickly and truncation changes the jumps only slightly, the stationary state stays near the ground state even on patches smaller than the light cone. We validate our approach numerically. On a grid of $81$ evolution times, the optimised filter reduces the worst-case heating response, or leakage, more than $116$-fold at equal cost. Across fifteen molecules and six chains, the cost falls by 27 to 56\% at matched design-grid leakage; at matched cost, the molecular leakage falls by a factor of $2.9$ to $2\times10^{3}$. Density-matrix simulations show high ground-state fidelity for both filters, and on Ising and Hubbard chains the cheaper filter keeps a ground-state population of at least $0.89$ on patches of three or four sites. The same patches fail on a Heisenberg chain whose truncation error falls more slowly with patch size and whose Lindbladian gap is 12 times smaller than the Ising chain's, pointing to a role for the gap in how far patches can be truncated. At fixed radius the per-branch cost becomes independent of system size, reducing the cost of dissipative state preparation.
summary: This paper details a novel, cost-optimized method for preparing the ground state of complex quantum systems using engineered dissipation. By combining linear programming with locality constraints derived from Lieb-Robinson bounds, the authors drastically reduce simulation errors and computational overhead compared to previous techniques. This advances the practical feasibility of quantum simulation for many-body physics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental challenge of preparing the ground state of a quantum many-body system using dissipative dynamics, while minimizing the computational cost associated with simulating the required quantum operations.
main_result: The authors introduce an optimized filter design that significantly reduces the worst-case heating response (leakage) by over 116-fold at equal cost, and achieves substantial cost reductions (up to 56%) across various molecular and chain systems.
method: The approach combines linear programming to optimize filter weights in the time domain with leveraging Lieb-Robinson bounds to restrict the required quantum evolution to local spatial patches.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum many-body Hamiltonians whose dynamics are driven to the ground state via a Lindbladian coupling to a bath. The analysis focuses on constructing and optimizing filtered jump operators that approximate the desired ground-state evolution.
key_observables: Ground-state fidelity, worst-case heating response (leakage), and computational cost (e.g., Toffolis per jump).
important_parameters: Spectral gap ($\Delta_{	ext{spec}}$), patch radius ($R$), and the time grid size ($T$).
main_assumptions: The cost model excludes outer loop overheads, and the locality-exploiting algorithms are distinct from the patch bounds used for the jump operators.
figures_summary: The notes reference tables comparing costs for different filter types (e.g., TFIM, Heisenberg) and showing scaling laws based on lattice size and constraints.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the problem (ground-state preparation) to proposing three key observations (LP optimization, Lieb-Robinson bounds, stability under truncation), culminating in numerical validation and cost analysis.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, resource-aware techniques for simulating open quantum systems, directly impacting the feasibility of quantum simulation algorithms for chemistry and materials science.
